keyChanges.title: AI5 Chip Tape-Out Complete but Production Significantly Delayed
keyChanges.description: Tesla completed AI5 chip tape-out on April 15, 2026, but high-volume production has been delayed to mid-to-late 2027, representing a near 2-year delay from original timelines. While initial samples and small volumes are expected in late 2026, full production requires several hundred thousand completed boards. This means meaningful deployment in vehicles will not occur until 2028 at earliest. Cybercab robotaxi will launch on AI4 hardware instead of AI5.

Dual-source manufacturing with TSMC and Samsung secured

keyChanges.title: Samsung $16.5B AI6 Chip Deal Secured but Timeline Slipping to 2028
keyChanges.description: Samsung signed an $8-year, $16.5 billion deal with Tesla in July 2025 to manufacture the AI6 chip at its Taylor, Texas facility using 2nm process. Equipment installation began April 24, 2026. However, AI6 tape-out is targeted for December 2026 with mass production pushed to mid-2028. This represents a 6-month delay from earlier 2027 estimates, indicating production challenges at the Taylor fab.

keyChanges.title: Dojo Supercomputer Project Shutdown Then Restarted; Strategic Uncertainty
keyChanges.description: Tesla discontinued the Dojo supercomputer team in August 2025, with Musk stating 'Dojo2 was an evolutionary dead end' and 'all technical paths converged on AI6.' However, in January 2026, Musk restarted the project as 'Dojo3' to build an all-in-house supercomputer using AI5 chips. This reversal indicates shifting strategic priorities and suggests continued uncertainty about AI chip architectural direction.

keyChanges.title: AI Chip Roadmap Acceleration Claims vs Reality: 9-Month Design Cadence Unproven
keyChanges.description: Elon Musk announced an aggressive 9-month chip design cycle targeting AI6 tape-out in December 2026 and AI7 planning already underway. However, AI5 took significantly longer than planned, and AI6 is targeting tape-out only in December 2026 (8+ months away from config date). The accelerated roadmap claims should be viewed skeptically given historical delays. No evidence yet that 9-month cycle is achievable.

keyChanges.title: Dual-Sourcing Strategy Confirmed for AI5 at TSMC Arizona & Samsung Texas
keyChanges.description: Tesla has confirmed dual-sourcing of AI5 chips between TSMC's Arizona facility and Samsung's Taylor, Texas plant using 4nm process (not 3nm as initially claimed). Both fabs produce the same design but use different transistor libraries and routing rules. This provides supply chain resilience but adds complexity and risks yield/performance variance between fabs.

keyChanges.title: Terafab $25B in-house chip factory announced; Timeline unrealistic
keyChanges.description: Elon Musk announced Tesla and SpaceX Terafab project, a $25B chip fabrication facility targeting 2nm and advanced nodes, claiming capability to run at '5-day cadence.' Initial site plans filed with Travis County include 2-million-square-foot facility in Taylor, Texas area. However, fab construction timelines typically span 3-5 years minimum, and Musk's '5-day' operation claim is not technically credible for advanced node fab.

keyChanges.title: Giga Berlin 4680 Capacity Doubled to 18 GWh with $250M Investment
keyChanges.description: On May 12, 2026, Giga Berlin plant manager André Thierig announced a $250 million investment to scale the factory's annual 4680 cell production capacity from 8 GWh to 18 GWh, more than doubling the previous target set in December 2025. Battery cell production at the Grünheide facility is projected to begin in H1 2027. This would support approximately 200,000 Model Y vehicles annually and reduce reliance on third-party cell suppliers.

keyChanges.title: Cell Giga Challenge Launched to Solve Manufacturing Scale Problems
keyChanges.description: Tesla launched the 'JUNI x Tesla Battery Cell Giga Challenge' in July 2026 with application deadline of July 24, 2026. The program targets startups with solutions for battery cell manufacturing in five key areas: materials, production, equipment, automation, and artificial intelligence. By opening this challenge, Tesla is publicly acknowledging it lacks internal technology solutions needed to reach 18 GWh capacity at Giga Berlin. Selected startups will receive paid pilot projects working directly with Tesla's 4680 team.

keyChanges.title: Dry Electrode Process Now Producing Both Anode and Cathode
keyChanges.description: Tesla confirmed in Q4 and FY 2025 update (reported January 28, 2026) that it is now producing 4680 cells whose anode and cathode are both manufactured using the dry electrode process. This represents a major technical achievement after years of development. Additionally, Tesla is developing four new dry-cathode 4680 variants (NC05, NC20, NC30, NC50) with the NC30 and NC50 featuring silicon-carbon anodes for increased energy density.

Tesla's in-house 4680 cells have achieved lowest-cost battery cell per kWh, beating suppliers like Panasonic and LG Energy Solution by end of 2024.

keyChanges.description: Tesla announced it produced its 100 millionth 4680 battery cell on September 14, 2024. The company had produced 50 million cells by June 5, 2024, meaning it doubled production in just over 3 months (101 days), averaging approximately 495,000 cells per day. This demonstrates accelerating production rates and manufacturing capability maturation.

keyChanges.title: Tesla announces Cybercab 'employee rides' at Giga Texas - parking lot only
keyChanges.description: On July 10, 2026, Tesla's Robotaxi account posted a video of a gold Cybercab driving across the Giga Texas outbound lot, with Tesla's main account quote-tweeting: 'Cybercab employee rides at Giga Texas starting soon.' However, the announcement is deliberately vague - Tesla gave no details on route, fleet size, or whether rides occur on public roads versus private factory property. Electrek reported on July 11 that the announcement appears to be nothing more than parking-lot ferries for employees, noting 'for any other automaker, our car drove an employee across the parking lot would not be a news event.' The announcement generated 2.9 million views but no substantive progress toward commercial deployment.

keyChanges.title: New Jersey bill threatens to ban Tesla's camera-only robotaxi statewide
keyChanges.description: On July 9, 2026, New Jersey's S1677 bill advanced, requiring robotaxis to use cameras plus lidar and radar - effectively banning Tesla's camera-only approach in the state. The bill establishes a three-year pilot program with mandatory multi-sensor requirements and a 50,000-mile in-state supervised-testing threshold before driverless commercial operation. State Senator Andrew Zwicker (physicist at Princeton Plasma Physics Lab) sponsored the bill after riding in a Waymo, citing safety concerns. Tesla lobbied aggressively against the bill, messaging New Jersey owners to flood Zwicker's office with ~4,000 protest emails in one day. The bill only targets commercial robotaxi fleets, not consumer FSD features, but represents a significant regulatory threat to Tesla's autonomy strategy in permissive East Coast markets.

keyChanges.title: Cybercab production ramps to 85-120+ units at Giga Texas, but deployment blocked
keyChanges.description: Drone footage captured between late June and July 10, 2026 shows Tesla has ramped Cybercab production to 85+ units staged at Gigafactory Texas, with some reports claiming counts exceeding 120 units. The Cybercab entered production in mid-February 2026, ahead of the April volume-production target. However, production capacity is not the constraint - EPA certification was secured May 26, 2026, but Tesla still lacks regulatory approval for autonomous operation in any jurisdiction. The vehicles remain in staging lots rather than deployed commercially. Meanwhile, the active robotaxi fleet (Model Y vehicles) has declined to just 34 vehicles total (20 active in last 7 days), down from a peak of ~165 in Dec 2025/Jan 2026. Software limitations via FSD v15 (expected Q4 2026 or Q1 2027) remain the fundamental blocker to scaling.

keyChanges.title: Tesla robotaxi fleet continues steady decline - down to 20 active vehicles
keyChanges.description: Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi fleet (Model Y vehicles) has collapsed to just 20 active vehicles (seen in last 7 days) as of July 2026, with total fleet at 34 authorized vehicles. This represents a 79% decline from the peak of ~165 vehicles in December 2025/January 2026. Austin dropped from 19 unsupervised vehicles to 14 active. Bay Area fleet cratered from 107 active vehicles in April to just 9. Dallas and Houston remain stuck at 3 vehicles each - the same tiny numbers from their April launch. The decline is attributed to safety concerns - Tesla's robotaxi crash rate sits between 4-9x higher than human drivers (one crash per 57,000 miles vs. human benchmark of one per 229,000 miles). Tesla is waiting for FSD v15 (Q4 2026 or Q1 2027) before scaling aggressively. Geographic expansion to Miami adds a 4th market but does not address the fundamental scaling failure.

keyChanges.title: Morgan Stanley forecasts 1,500 robotaxis by end of 2026 - but current fleet at 20
keyChanges.description: Morgan Stanley published analysis on July 6, 2026 projecting Tesla's robotaxi fleet will grow to 1,500 vehicles by year-end 2026 and 30,000 by 2030. The bank expects launches in Phoenix, Orlando, Tampa, Las Vegas, and possibly New Orleans by Q4 2026. However, this projection appears highly optimistic given the current reality: Tesla's active fleet is just 20 vehicles (34 total authorized) as of July 2026, down from 165 at peak. To reach 1,500 vehicles by December 31, 2026 would require adding ~1,480 vehicles in 6 months (~247 vehicles/month or ~8 vehicles/day) - a 75x scale-up from current levels. Tesla has explicitly stated it is waiting for FSD v15 (Q4 2026 or Q1 2027) before scaling, and safety data shows crash rates 4-9x higher than human drivers. Morgan Stanley maintains Equalweight rating and $415 price target.

keyChanges.title: Tesla showcases Cybercab accessibility features at National Federation of the Blind convention
keyChanges.description: On July 3, 2026, Tesla brought the Cybercab to the National Federation of the Blind (NFB) Annual Convention at the JW Marriott Austin to demonstrate accessibility features for blind and visually impaired users. The vehicle includes Braille lettering on door releases and emergency stop button, dedicated space for service animals and assistive devices, wheelchair-height seating, and external microphones/speakers for audible arrival announcements and verbal destination commands. Attendees experienced the steering-wheel-free design firsthand. The demo highlights Tesla's focus on inclusive autonomous mobility for ~2.2 million blind Americans (plus millions more with vision impairment). However, the event is primarily PR-focused - the Cybercab still lacks regulatory approval for autonomous operation in any jurisdiction, and deployment remains blocked until FSD v15 in Q4 2026 or Q1 2027.

keyChanges.title: NHTSA escalates FSD investigation to Engineering Analysis covering 3.2M vehicles
keyChanges.description: On March 19, 2026, NHTSA upgraded its Tesla FSD probe from a Preliminary Evaluation to a formal Engineering Analysis (EA26002) covering 3.2 million vehicles across all Tesla models. The investigation found that FSD's camera-based system fails to detect common road conditions that impair visibility—sun glare and fog—and doesn't adequately warn drivers before crashes occur. The probe involves at least nine documented crashes, including one fatal pedestrian collision and another crash resulting in injury. This escalation is the stage that typically precedes a mandatory recall, representing significant regulatory risk.

sentiment.headline: neutral
sentiment.rationale: While headlines focus on 'investigation escalation,' the reality is NHTSA moved to the pre-recall stage due to fundamental safety failures in FSD's vision system. The system's inability to detect degraded visibility from common conditions (glare, fog) and failure to warn drivers until just before impact represents a core architectural problem affecting 3.2M vehicles.

keyChanges.title: Sweden formally recommends EU reject FSD approval unless speed offset removed
keyChanges.description: Sweden's transport authority formally recommended to the EU's Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) that the bloc votes against EU-wide rollout of Tesla FSD unless the Speed Offset feature is removed. The feature allows vehicles to exceed posted speed limits by a driver-defined margin. In a letter dated April 30, 2026, Sweden stated that 'allowing automated systems to systematically exceed legal speed limits risks undermining both the legal framework and the expected safety benefits of vehicle automation.' This represents a major roadblock for EU-wide approval, as the qualified majority requires 15 of 27 member states representing 65% of EU population, effectively requiring Germany, France or Italy's support.

sentiment.headline: neutral
sentiment.rationale: Sweden's formal objection to TCMV represents a significant regulatory barrier to EU-wide approval. Without major market support (Germany, France, Italy), Tesla faces continued fragmentation requiring country-by-country approvals rather than streamlined EU-wide access.

keyChanges.title: Germany approves FSD, becomes 6th European country with rollout on May 22
keyChanges.description: Germany approved FSD Supervised and began rolling it out to subscribers on May 22, 2026. The approval leveraged the Netherlands' RDW provisional EU type approval for FSD under UN Regulation 171, with Germany's federal vehicle authority (KBA) adopting that approval. The version rolling out is FSD v14 via software update 2026.8.6, supporting both Hardware 3 and Hardware 4 vehicles. Germany's approval validates the EU mutual recognition pathway as a viable fast-track mechanism, providing precedent for France, Italy, Spain, and other member states.

sentiment.headline: positive
sentiment.rationale: Germany's approval represents Tesla's largest European market gaining FSD access and validates the mutual recognition pathway. However, this is still individual country approval rather than EU-wide deployment, requiring continued country-by-country activation.

keyChanges.title: Belgium approves FSD on June 10, becomes 5th European country
keyChanges.description: Belgium became the 13th country globally and 5th in Europe to receive official approval for FSD Supervised on June 10, 2026. Flemish Mobility Minister Annick De Ridder signed the official approval after Tesla completed extensive supervised testing on Flemish public roads, including the required 5,000 km benchmark. The approval leverages the Dutch RDW's provisional European type approval under UN Regulation 171. Initial rollout is exclusive to Hardware 4 vehicles, featuring FSD v14 tailored for European roads. Pricing is set at €99/month, with a reduced €49/month rate for Enhanced Autopilot owners.

sentiment.headline: positive
sentiment.rationale: Belgium's approval demonstrates continued European expansion momentum, but the approval came just one day after Denmark, highlighting the country-by-country fragmentation. The pattern shows Tesla making progress but still far from streamlined EU-wide deployment.

keyChanges.title: Tesla FSD v14 Lite rollout begins for HW3 vehicles starting July 1
keyChanges.description: Tesla began rolling out FSD v14 Lite (software update 2026.20.5.1) to Hardware 3 (HW3) vehicles starting July 1, 2026, initially to Early Access Group members. This represents the first FSD v14 deployment to the installed base of approximately 4 million older Tesla vehicles that cannot run full FSD v14. The 'Lite' version includes Start Self-Driving from Park, Arrival Options (parking lot, street, driveway, curbside), Speed Profiles, and UI improvements. By July 10, Tesla AI confirmed v14 Lite rollout to early access HW3 owners in South Korea, marking the first HW3 FSD deployment outside North America. Current FSD v14 updates in July include v14.3.3 (2026.14.6.x) with improvements to responsiveness across navigation, merges, pedestrians, traffic lights, and smoother steering.

sentiment.headline: positive
sentiment.rationale: FSD v14 Lite rollout to HW3 addresses a large installed base (~4M vehicles) that was excluded from v14. However, this is a reduced-capability 'Lite' version, and the rollout started over 6 months after v14 launched on HW4. The fact Tesla needed to create a separate 'Lite' version underscores HW3's computational limitations and Tesla's April 2026 confirmation that HW3 cannot achieve unsupervised FSD.

keyChanges.title: Finland signals potential FSD approval before October EU vote
keyChanges.description: Finland's transport authority Traficom indicated it may approve Tesla FSD Supervised before the EU-wide decision expected at the October 2026 TCMV meeting. Traficom stated FSD has 'strong safety potential' and is prepared to move forward after summer 2026, contingent on Tesla providing additional information in three areas: driver retake time (how quickly a driver can reassume control), overtaking performance, and the speed-offset feature. Notably, Finnish regulators stated that speeding is already common in Finland and the speed offset is 'justified on the grounds that the driver must be given sufficient flexibility,' contrasting sharply with Sweden's opposition. Approximately 6,500 Finnish vehicles are already equipped with FSD hardware (~0.24% of Finland's 2.7M passenger vehicles).

sentiment.rationale: Finland's positive assessment and willingness to approve before October represents regulatory progress. However, the approval is conditional on Tesla answering outstanding technical questions, and Finland's position on speed offset contrasts with Sweden's formal objection, highlighting continued EU regulatory fragmentation.

keyChanges.title: Tesla Model Y first vehicle to pass NHTSA's new ADAS safety tests
keyChanges.description: The 2026 Tesla Model Y became the first vehicle to pass NHTSA's new benchmark for vehicles equipped with advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), announced May 7, 2026. Model Y units manufactured on or after November 12, 2025, successfully met criteria for four newly integrated ADAS tests: pedestrian automatic emergency braking, lane keeping assistance, blind spot warning, and blind spot intervention, plus four original ADAS criteria (forward collision warning, crash imminent braking, dynamic brake support, lane departure warning). However, this achievement for basic ADAS features comes amid NHTSA's escalated Engineering Analysis investigation (EA26002) into Tesla's 'Full Self-Driving' system covering 3.2 million vehicles—the stage that typically precedes a recall.

sentiment.headline: positive
sentiment.rationale: Headlines celebrate Model Y passing ADAS tests, but the reality is this achievement covers basic driver assistance features while NHTSA simultaneously investigates FSD for fundamental safety failures in reduced visibility. The contrast highlights the gap between Tesla's basic ADAS capabilities (which passed) and FSD Supervised (which is under pre-recall investigation).

keyChanges.title: California DMV confirms Tesla compliance after Autopilot branding dropped
keyChanges.description: The California DMV confirmed Tesla's 'corrective action' on February 17, 2026, after Tesla stopped using the term 'Autopilot' in its marketing. In December 2025, a California judge ruled that Tesla's use of 'Autopilot' to describe ADAS features is misleading and violates state law, finding that the naming 'follows a long but unlawful tradition of intentionally using ambiguity to mislead consumers.' Tesla renamed Autopilot to 'Traffic Aware Cruise Control' and consistently uses 'Full Self-Driving (Supervised)' even when abbreviating to FSD. This compliance avoided a 30-day suspension of Tesla's dealer and manufacturer licenses in California.

sentiment.headline: neutral
sentiment.rationale: While headlines frame this as compliance and avoiding a ban, the reality is a California judge ruled Tesla's marketing was intentionally misleading and violated state law. Tesla was forced to rebrand core features to avoid license suspension—a significant regulatory and reputational setback confirming years of misleading marketing practices.

keyChanges.title: Tesla confirms FSD v15 delayed to end-2026/early-2027; robotaxi scale blocked until release
keyChanges.description: During the Q1 2026 earnings call (April 22, 2026), Tesla confirmed FSD v15 will not ship until late 2026 or early 2027, representing a delay of the 10x parameter model upgrade that was originally planned for v14 in late 2025. CEO Elon Musk explicitly stated large-scale robotaxi expansion will NOT proceed until v15 is released, citing the need for 'major architectural improvements' to reach required safety levels. This confirms v15 is the critical blocker for both unsupervised FSD and robotaxi commercialization. The 10-billion-parameter model is described as a 'total architectural overhaul' designed to achieve 'orders of magnitude beyond human capability' safety. While v15 will run on Hardware 4 (no upgrade needed), the ~9-12 month delay from original v14 timeline pushes Tesla's autonomy roadmap into 2027.

sentiment.headline: neutral
sentiment.rationale: Headlines emphasize HW4 compatibility (positive framing), but reality is a 9-12 month delay of the critical model upgrade, pushing robotaxi scale and unsupervised FSD into 2027. This is the second major delay (originally v14 late-2025, now v15 end-2026/early-2027). Robotaxi expansion explicitly blocked until v15 ships.

keyChanges.title: Tesla confirms Hardware 3 cannot support unsupervised FSD or v15; 4M vehicles left behind
keyChanges.description: On April 22-23, 2026 (Q1 earnings call), Tesla officially confirmed that Hardware 3 (HW3) vehicles—approximately 4 million globally—cannot and will not support unsupervised Full Self-Driving or FSD v15. Elon Musk cited hardware limitations: HW3 has 'only one eighth of the memory bandwidth of Hardware 4' and lacks the compute/memory capacity for the 10-billion-parameter v15 model. FSD v14 Lite is confirmed as the 'ultimate ceiling version' for HW3 hardware. This directly contradicts Tesla's 2016-2019 promises that HW3 would support full autonomy. Tesla is offering affected customers (many who paid $8,000-15,000 for FSD) either: (1) discounted trade-in to HW4 vehicle, or (2) paid hardware upgrade requiring replacement of computer AND all cameras. This represents a broken promise to millions of early FSD adopters and a material limitation on Tesla's addressable autonomy market.

keyChanges.title: Tesla robotaxi fleet stagnates at 20-25 vehicles after 1 year; scaling failure evident as expansion blocked until v15
keyChanges.description: As of June-July 2026, Tesla's unsupervised robotaxi fleet remains stuck at approximately 20-25 active vehicles across Austin, Dallas, and Houston—one full year after the June 2025 Austin launch. Multiple reports indicate the fleet has actually shrunk from 25 vehicles in April 2026 to 20 vehicles by June 2026. The service area expanded to entire Austin metro in June, but vehicle count did not scale. This represents a clear scaling failure: after 12 months of operation, Tesla cannot grow the fleet beyond ~25 vehicles. Safety concerns are evident: the Austin fleet logged 14 crashes in first 7 months (~800K miles), a rate 4x worse than average US driver per Tesla's own benchmarks (1 crash per 57K miles vs 1 per 229K miles). Elon Musk confirmed on Q1 call that large-scale expansion is blocked until FSD v15 (late-2026/early-2027), effectively admitting current v14 is not safe enough to scale. Preparations for Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, Las Vegas remain in 'preparation' stage with no active deployments.

sentiment.headline: positive
sentiment.rationale: Headlines tout 'expansion to entire Austin metro' and 'preparations for new cities,' but reality is fleet stuck/shrinking at 20-25 vehicles after 1 full year. This is a failed scaling attempt. Tesla is blocking expansion due to safety concerns (4x crash rate vs human drivers) and admitting v14 inadequate. One year with no meaningful fleet growth = negative.

keyChanges.title: Tesla rolls out FSD v14 Lite to Hardware 3 vehicles in late June; international expansion underway
keyChanges.description: Starting June 29, 2026, Tesla began rolling out FSD v14 Lite (firmware 2026.20.5.1) to Hardware 3 vehicles, ending a 16-month wait for 4 million HW3 owners since v13 was the last major update they received. The v14 Lite update uses 'distillation' technology to compress HW4's v14 capabilities onto HW3's limited hardware, bringing improvements to navigation, merges, pedestrian interactions, traffic lights, parking/unparking, and arrival options. Tesla's AI chief Ashok Elluswamy confirmed rollout started with early access drivers, with wider release planned 'over the next few weeks.' International rollout also began, with South Korea becoming the first non-US market to receive FSD v14 Lite. However, v14 Lite remains Level 2 supervised (hands-on required) and is confirmed as the 'ultimate ceiling version' for HW3—unsupervised FSD will never come to HW3 hardware. While this is a functional improvement for HW3 owners, it does not change the fundamental limitation: HW3 is excluded from Tesla's autonomy roadmap (unsupervised FSD, v15, robotaxi).

sentiment.headline: positive
sentiment.rationale: Headlines celebrate 'FSD v14 finally arrives for HW3' after 16-month wait, but reality is more nuanced: v14 Lite is a downscaled version (not full v14), remains supervised Level 2, and is the ceiling for HW3 (no unsupervised future). It's a functional improvement but confirms HW3's permanent exclusion from autonomy. Mixed signals: progress for near-term, dead-end for long-term.

keyChanges.title: Musk warns Optimus production will be 'extremely slow' as July start approaches
keyChanges.description: On July 1, 2026, Elon Musk visited the Optimus production line at Fremont and shared a team photo, responding to speculation by stating 'Optimus production will be extremely slow at first because everything is new.' This directly contradicts earlier optimism and occurs just weeks before the planned late July/August production start. Musk emphasized 'this is not like making a car' due to 10,000 unique parts. Production is expected to ramp from dozens per week in June to 100-150 per week in July, 300 per week in August, and a target of 1,000 units per week by September 2026 according to supplier reports. However, all 2026 units will be for internal testing only, not commercial customers.

sentiment.headline: neutral
sentiment.rationale: Musk's 'extremely slow' warning just weeks before production start signals significant challenges. Despite supplier targets of 1,000 units/week by September, Musk's public caution indicates these are aspirational. The reality is Tesla missed 2025 targets entirely (aimed for ~10,000 units, delivered zero commercial units), and current deployed units do no productive work. 'Everything is new' admission shows unproven production process at scale.

keyChanges.title: Terafab Execution Risks: Semiconductor Inexperience, Talent Shortage, and Yield Challenges
keyChanges.description: Critical analysis reveals Terafab faces severe execution risks that threaten the $25B+ investment. Tesla has no semiconductor manufacturing experience. The company is advancing 6+ simultaneous chip projects (AI-related, Dojo-related, SpaceX satellites) while attempting vertical integration across mask design, logic, memory, and advanced packaging. Analysts cite lack of talent and time as primary constraints. The biggest technical challenge is controlling yields at advanced 2nm nodes—transistor architecture has shifted to GAAFET, requiring significant upgrades to materials, equipment, and process modules. Even minor deviations could cause sharp yield drops.
